hints: First find the extension by comparing the stretched and unstretched spring lengths, then read the force at that extension from Fig. 3.1.
The elastic potential energy is the area under a straight force-extension graph, so use the area of a triangle.
walkthrough: The extension is 0.72 m − 0.40 m = 0.32 m.
From Fig. 3.1, the force at an extension of 0.32 m is 4.0 N.
The elastic potential energy is the triangular area under the force-extension graph: E_P = ½Fx.

hints: The block moves downward by the same 0.32 m through which the spring extends.
Because the weight is given directly, use the magnitude of the energy decrease as weight multiplied by vertical distance.
walkthrough: The block moves downward by 0.72 m − 0.40 m = 0.32 m.
The magnitude of the gravitational potential energy decrease is WΔh, equivalently mgΔh.
The gravitational potential energy decreases by 0.80 J.

hints: With air resistance negligible, compare the gravitational potential energy lost with the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
The energy not stored elastically is the block's kinetic energy.
walkthrough: The block loses 0.80 J of gravitational potential energy.
The spring gains 0.64 J of elastic potential energy.
With no energy dissipated, the remaining energy is kinetic energy: E_K = 0.80 − 0.64 = 0.16 J.

hints: Use the 0.16 J kinetic energy from part (b)(i) and convert the stated weight into mass before using the kinetic-energy relationship.
Rearrange E_K = ½mv² to make v the subject, then take the square root only after substituting the mass.
walkthrough: The block mass is m = W / g = 2.5 / 9.81 = 0.255 kg.
Use E_K = ½mv² with E_K = 0.16 J: 0.16 = ½(2.5 / 9.81)v².
The speed of the block is 1.1 m s⁻¹.
